# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles decimal coordinates, hydrological basin assignments, primary bibliographic citations and multi-period population series for 199 individually assessed prehistoric settlements across Sub-Saharan Africa between 10000BC and 1000BC. Screened from 201 candidate rockshelters, coastal shellmiddens, lakeside fishing camps, pastoral homesteads and early mudbrick or dry-stone towns (2 excluded), the retained sites span 39 modern jurisdictions and 637 dated population observations across sixteen HydroBASINS Level 6 catchments. Active recorded loci rise from 41 early Holocene camps at 9000BC and 75 at 7000BC to 85 at 5000BC, 109 at 3000BC and 111 at 2000BC before consolidating to 45 larger nucleated villages and fortified towns at 1000BC, tracing site sizes from small foraging shelters of 15 to 90 inhabitants up to Dakhlet el Atrous (6,84k) and Kerma (14,7k).



# Methodology

## Screening, Radiocarbon Anchors and HydroBASINS Grouping

Candidate prehistoric loci were compiled from excavated cave sequences, regional surface surveys, radiocarbon compendia including p3k14c, XRONOS and OSAAR, and published regional monographs [@BIRD2022P3K14C; @Hinz2023XRONOS; @Besse2020OSAAR; @Boisard2024CriticalInventory; @Phillipson2005AfricanArch]. Screening 201 initial entries removed 2 duplicate or non-habitation records, retaining 199 individually assessed sites across 39 jurisdictions (38 in the Nubian Nile, Atbara and Sudd alone). Each entry is mapped by its decimal coordinates onto the 16 HydroBASINS Level 6 macro-catchments clipped to geoBoundaries territorial masks [@LehnerGrill2013HydroBASINS; @Runfola2020GeoBoundaries].

Site population trajectories reflect excavated habitation areas, compound enclosures, midden volumes and cave floor capacities converted using period-appropriate hunter-gatherer, pastoral and agropastoral density coefficients [@Goldstein2025CulturalEconomic; @Marks2026TheHolocene; @Humphris2017NewRadiocarbon; @Mcintosh1988FromStone]. Because archaeological occupation spans vary between regions, Tables 1 to 16 display linearly interpolated resident counts at four continental benchmarks (7000BC, 4000BC, 2000BC and 1000BC) alongside each site's exact assessed peak, peak date and primary bibliographic source, marking pre-foundation or post-abandonment benchmarks with a hyphen (-).

## Rank-Size Distribution and Spatial Coverage

Across all 199 individually assessed sites, rank-size regression on the upper 99 settlements conforms closely to Zipf scaling with an exponent of $q = 1,05$ ($R^2 = 0,985$; Figure \ref{fig:settlements-rank}), while full-sample scaling yields a tail slope of 1,35 ($R^2 = 0,94$) reflecting the wide base of Later Stone Age foraging rockshelters below 60 inhabitants [@Mitchell2015DiscontinuitiesHunter; @Will2022CoastalAdaptations; @Dusseldorp2013PleistoceneHomo]. Every one of the 16 HydroBASINS catchments contains between 2 and 38 dated settlements with zero unpopulated basins.

# Results

## Nubian Nile, Atbara and Sudd Wetlands

Table \ref{tab:sr-nile} catalogues 38 individually assessed settlements along the Nile cataracts, Wadi Howar, Gash delta and Sudd marshes. Early Khartoum Mesolithic fishing settlements such as Abu Darbein, Aneibis, Saggai and El Barga gave way to Neolithic pastoral villages at El Kadero, El Kadada, R12 and Esh Shaheinab, culminating in the Kingdom of Kush capital at Kerma (14,7k) and Egyptian fortified towns at Buhen (3,85k), Sai Island (3,47k), Napata (2,85k) and Amara West (2,34k) [@Humphris2017NewRadiocarbon; @Phillipson2005AfricanArch; @Adriansen2000TheDevelopment].

# Limitations

Three limitations govern interpretation of this prehistoric settlement ledger. First, caves, rockshelters and dry-stone escarpment walls preserve far better than open-air wooden camps in humid rainforests or seasonally flooded plains, biasing raw site counts toward Nubia and southern Africa relative to the Congo basin [@Will2024TheGeneric; @KarenDLupo1889IntensiveLate; @Boisard2024CriticalInventory]. Second, site-level population figures carry 30% to 50% uncertainty where seasonal band aggregation cannot be separated cleanly from year-round occupation [@Mitchell2015DiscontinuitiesHunter; @Goldstein2025CulturalEconomic; @Marks2026TheHolocene]. Third, because the 199 retained sites document excavated loci rather than the full dispersed foraging and pastoral landscape, their combined sums represent attested site populations and must be read alongside the basin-wide totals in the companion review [@BIRD2022P3K14C; @Hinz2023XRONOS].

# Conclusion

Taken together, the 199 individually assessed settlements document nine millennia of Sub-Saharan prehistory across 39 modern jurisdictions and 16 HydroBASINS catchments [@LehnerGrill2013HydroBASINS; @Runfola2020GeoBoundaries]. They trace how early Holocene aquatic camps and southern African rockshelters coexisted with Saharan pastoralism before mid-Holocene desiccation concentrated population into Nubian towns around Kerma and stone-walled Sahelian villages along the Dhar Tichitt escarpment ahead of the Iron Age [@Humphris2017NewRadiocarbon; @Mcintosh1988FromStone; @Toba2026EmergenceSocial].
